meta.title: Who really said "Physics is like sex: sure, it may give some practical results, but that's not why we do it"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in Feynman's books or biographies. The oldest printed use anyone has found is a 2000 popular-science book, where it sits beside a fake Einstein line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Physics is like sex: sure, it may give some practical results, but that's not why we do it'?
meta.ogDescription: The best-known Feynman one-liner he probably never said. No book, lecture or biography carries it; the trail runs out in a 2000 paperback.

answer.label: Not Richard Feynman — no source has ever surfaced
answer.sourceLine: The line is repeated everywhere as Feynman’s and rests on nothing. It appears in none of his books and in no biography of him, and the earliest printed use Wikiquote’s editors could find is a 2000 popular-science paperback by the ABC science broadcaster Robyn Williams — which introduces it immediately after a saying Einstein also never said. Two unsourced quips in one sentence is the signature of a quote that was assembled rather than recorded.

source.heading: Where the trail runs out

docMeta.dd: Robyn Williams, ABC science broadcaster; Sydney: University of New South Wales Press, 2000

source.excerpt: Einstein said, ‘You do not really understand something unless you can explain it to your grandmother’. Richard Feynman added, ‘Physics is like sex: sure, it may give some practical results, but that’s not why we do it’.
trail: The disputed section of Feynman’s Wikiquote entry states plainly that the line ‘does not appear to be from any of his books or cited in a biography’, and that a Google Books search puts the oldest book citing ‘physics is like sex’ at Scary Monsters and Bright Ideas (2000) by the science broadcaster Robyn Williams the disputed entry ↗.

The company it keeps is the strongest signal against it. On that page the quip is introduced directly after ‘You do not really understand something unless you can explain it to your grandmother’, credited to Einstein — a saying Einstein is not documented as having said. Wikiquote’s own reasoning runs the same way: given the first is not genuine, the second is unlikely to be the reasoning ↗.

We also checked Quote Investigator, which has traced a large share of the fake Feynman and Einstein canon: it has no article on this line, so no specialist has pushed the trail back beyond the 2000 book or turned up a Feynman source. The nearest thing to a positive case appears on the Wikiquote talk page, where an editor recalls Leonard Susskind attributing a cruder version to Feynman in a lecture series — and says outright that they cannot place which lecture, so it cannot be sourced either the talk-page discussion ↗.

The book itself is real and datable: the Internet Archive holds Scary Monsters and Bright Ideas, University of New South Wales Press, 2000. It is lending-restricted, so we could not open page 44 to confirm the transcription above the edition record ↗.
source.cutTag: Scary Monsters and Bright Ideas, 2000, p. 44

We were not able to read page 44 ourselves — the Internet Archive’s copy of the book is lending-restricted — so the wording and page here are Wikiquote’s, reported as theirs rather than confirmed against the printed page.

author.name: Richard Feynman
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Feynman
author.bio: Richard Feynman (1918–1988) shared the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics for quantum electrodynamics and cultivated a public character — bongo player, safecracker, teller of stories against himself — that made him the natural home for any joke a physicist might plausibly tell. He wrote a great deal, and much of it is funny. None of it contains this line.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared physics quips on the internet, and one of the least documented. The case against it is not that someone else said it — it is that nobody can show anyone saying it.

items.why: Wikiquote’s disputed section states the line ‘does not appear to be from any of his books or cited in a biography’. No lecture transcript, essay or interview has been produced for it the disputed entry ↗.

items.who: The oldest printing found, not the origin
items.why: Robyn Williams’s book quotes the line as Feynman’s rather than claiming it, so it marks where the paper trail currently begins, not where the sentence came from. Wikiquote reached it by a Google Books search, and no earlier printing has been produced since the citation ↗.

items.who: The other half of the same passage, also unsourced
items.why: The sentence immediately before it on page 44 credits Einstein with ‘you do not really understand something unless you can explain it to your grandmother’, which is itself not documented in Einstein. A pairing of two undocumented quips is the shape of received wisdom, not of a record.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has produced a source. The line is absent from Feynman’s books, lectures and biographies, and the trail ends at a 2000 popular-science paperback that was already quoting it as his Wikiquote, disputed ↗.

context.heading: Why it sounds like him
lead: The joke is well made. It defends curiosity against the demand that research justify itself by its applications, and it does so in the register Feynman actually used — deflating, slightly rude, on the side of pleasure. He genuinely did argue that the point of physics is the finding out; The Pleasure of Finding Things Out is a title he put his name to.

That is exactly why the attribution is hard to dislodge. The line is not out of character, it is too much in character — a quip built to sound like Feynman, attached to him at some point before 2000, and repeated ever since by people with no more evidence than the fact that it fits.
context.detailsSummary: What has and has not been checked
detailsBody: Not found: any Feynman book, lecture transcript, interview or biography containing the line.
Found: Scary Monsters and Bright Ideas (2000), p. 44, quoting it as his — the oldest printing Wikiquote’s editors located via Google Books.
Also unsourced: the Einstein ‘explain it to your grandmother’ line printed beside it on the same page.
No Quote Investigator article exists for this quip, so no specialist has traced it further back.
Not established: who wrote it, or when it was first attached to Feynman.
context.pull: The case against it is not that someone else said it. It is that nobody can show anyone saying it.
